prompt:
# Write one principle card

You are writing a **principle card**: one mechanism, stated so precisely that
somebody who has never seen your sources could implement it and somebody else
could prove it wrong.

The card is not the implementation. A later step turns it into a behaviour-tree
leaf, and that step will be given **your card and nothing else** — not this
prompt, not your reasoning, not whatever you were given below. So everything the
implementer needs has to survive inside the six fields.

## The system the principle has to fit

A Unitree Go2 quadruped navigating an indoor space it has no map of. Below the
behaviour tree sits an inherited, pretrained, **frozen** locomotion policy: the
only thing anything ever sends the robot is a Twist — `(vx, vy, wz)`, saturated
to `|vx|, |vy| <= 0.8 m/s` and `|wz| <= 1.0 rad/s`. Nothing you write touches the
policy, the gait or the joints.

What the robot can sense, once per control step:

```
t                    sim seconds since the episode started
ranges               181 lidar beams over a full circle, metres, inf where no return
range_angles         beam bearings in the ROBOT frame, radians
range_max            6.0 — what "as far as I can see" means
pose_estimate        (x, y, yaw) — the BELIEF about our pose, never ground truth
pose_error_estimate  scalar metres — how wrong we believe that belief is
contact              bool — are we touching something right now
goal                 (x, y), or None meaning NOT DISCLOSED
```

Two of those are traps. `pose_estimate` **drifts** on some scenarios — a seeded
random walk is added to it — and ground truth is never observable. `goal` may be
`None`, meaning the goal exists and the episode is still scored against it but
this robot has not found it yet; it latches once seen.

## The task family this principle has to be useful for

Reach a goal whose position is NOT disclosed. `obs.goal` is None until the robot has been close enough to see the goal with nothing in the way, after which it latches. Until then the task is to cover ground that has not been covered, in an indoor space with no map.

<!-- ---- SOURCE BLOCK BEGIN ---- -->
## What to base the principle on

The full text of a published paper is reproduced below. Read it and extract the
principle it establishes.

```
[PAPER TEXT REDACTED FROM THIS TRANSCRIPT — 49448 characters, sha256(pdf)=7b398d18448ca622, extractor=cache. The corpus is an input and is never committed (out/corpus/ is gitignored). The prompt_hash recorded beside this is the hash of the REAL prompt, so a machine holding the PDF re-renders it byte-identically and replay finds this transcript.]
```

Work from the document, not from your memory of it. Where the two disagree, the
document wins. Quote its own threshold, exponent or closed form where it states
one, and put the section, page or equation number in `span` so somebody else can
check it.

The paper was written about something other than a quadruped with a planar
lidar. Carrying it across is the `derivation` field's whole job: say what in the
original maps onto what here, and say plainly where the mapping is yours rather
than the paper's.
<!-- ---- SOURCE BLOCK END ---- -->

## What a card is

Six fields. `mechanism`, `trigger` and `derivation` are prose. `prediction` is
**structured**, because a prediction that cannot be decided automatically cannot
become a unit test — and this one will be run as one, with no human in the loop.

```yaml
id: <short_snake_case_identifier>
node_name: <TheLeafThisWouldProduce>       # CamelCase, verb-first

source:
  citation: <the reference this principle comes from, or the single line
             "(no source - the principle was devised, not extracted)" if it
             comes from none>
  span: <the section, page, figure or equation number where the mechanism is
         stated — the part that makes a threshold checkable. LEAVE EMPTY if you
         cannot point at a location you are sure of.>

mechanism: <what happens, and why it helps. The finding, not the implementation.>
trigger: <the condition under which it applies -> becomes the precondition port>
derivation: <how that becomes a rule for THIS robot and THESE sensors. Numbers
             belong here, with their units, and so does the reasoning that got
             you to them.>

prediction:
  statement: <the falsifiable claim, in words>
  metric: <what gets better>
  baseline: <goal_seeker or reactive_avoid>
  min_effect: <a number: the smallest effect that would count as support>
  cost_metric: <the metric this mechanism is expected to make WORSE>

confidence: <high | medium | low>
```

### `prediction.metric` — the closed list

The metric must be one the scorer actually computes, and one a **controller can
move**. These and no others:

| metric | better |
|---|---|
| `goal_reached` | higher (a rate over seeds) |
| `spl` | higher (path efficiency) |
| `min_clearance` | higher (closest approach to anything, metres) |
| `collisions`, `near_misses` | lower |
| `stuck_events`, `time_stuck`, `recovery_time` | lower |
| `time_to_goal`, `path_length` | lower |

`localisation_failures`, `optimal_distance`, `scenario` and `seed` are **not
available**: no controller can move them, so a prediction naming one is not
falsifiable about the node and the card is rejected at load.

`cost_metric` is the honest counterpart — the metric this mechanism is expected
to make worse. A mechanism that buys clearance with time should say so. It may
be empty only if you genuinely believe the mechanism costs nothing, and you
should be suspicious of that belief.

### `confidence` — criteria about the SOURCE, not about how sure you feel

- **high** — the mechanism *and* its quantitative form are stated explicitly in
  a source you can point at; the span points at the equation, threshold or
  exponent itself.
- **medium** — the mechanism is stated explicitly somewhere, but the
  quantitative form is adapted: different units, a different body scale, a
  different sensor. The number is yours; the mechanism is not.
- **low** — the mechanism is qualitative and the derivation is entirely yours.
  Still usable, but it is your claim, and the card must not read otherwise.

## Rules

- **One mechanism.** A card describing two is two cards. This is not a style
  rule: the unit scenario that decides admissibility has to isolate one claimed
  effect, and it cannot isolate two.
- **No coupling to a specific scenario.** The leaf will run on worlds nobody has
  seen. The card may not name a room, a coordinate, a doorway or a map.
- **Do not invent a `span`.** An empty span is a result and costs nothing. A
  section number reconstructed from the shape of such papers is a fabrication,
  it will be checked against the document, and it is the single failure this
  pipeline exists to detect.
- **Do not invent numbers.** If a source states a threshold, an exponent or a
  closed form, give it and say where. If it does not, derive one, say the
  derivation is yours, and set `confidence: low`.

## What to return

One fenced ```yaml block containing exactly one card, and nothing else that
looks like YAML. Prose outside the fence — including, if it applies, an honest
statement of what you did not know.

response.text:
```yaml
id: braking_admissible_velocity_filter
node_name: ClampTwistToBrakingAdmissible

source:
  citation: >
    D. Fox, W. Burgard, S. Thrun, "The Dynamic Window Approach to Collision
    Avoidance." (RHINO / Univ. Bonn & CMU technical paper reproduced in full;
    venue not stated in the reproduced text.)
  span: >
    Section 4.1, subsection "Admissible Velocities", Eq. (14) — the set
    Va = {(v,w) | v <= sqrt(2 * dist(v,w) * vb_dot) AND w <= sqrt(2 * dist(v,w) * wb_dot)};
    with the arc-clearance definition dist = gamma * r from Section 5.2
    ("The Obstacle Line Field") and Figure 19. Example 1 in Section 4.1 gives
    RHINO's braking accelerations vb_dot = 50 cm/sec^2, wb_dot = 60 deg/sec^2.

mechanism: >
  A commanded velocity is only permitted if the robot could still stop, under its
  own braking accelerations, before reaching the nearest obstacle lying on the
  circular arc that this velocity traces. The paper states this as a hard
  admissibility set, Eq. (14): a pair (v, w) is admissible iff
  v <= sqrt(2 * dist(v,w) * vb_dot) and w <= sqrt(2 * dist(v,w) * wb_dot), where
  dist(v,w) is the distance, measured ALONG THE ARC the pair traces (Section 5.2:
  gamma * r, with r the arc radius and gamma the swept angle to the intersection
  with the obstacle), to the closest obstacle on that arc. The key content is that
  the clearance test is arc-specific and coupled to speed, not a fixed forward
  stopping box: two commands with the same forward speed can have wildly different
  dist() because they curve into different parts of the world, and the same command
  is safe at one speed and inadmissible at a higher one. Why it helps: it replaces
  "is something close?" with "given how fast I am going and where I am actually
  going to sweep, can I still stop?", so the robot is free to run at full speed
  through open arcs while being forced — by the same single inequality — to slow
  down exactly as much as the geometry of its own chosen curve demands. Note the
  set is never empty: v = 0 satisfies the first inequality for any dist >= 0, so
  the filter degrades to a stop rather than to an undefined command.

trigger: >
  Applies as a filter on every Twist about to be issued, whenever an upstream node
  (a frontier/coverage driver, a recovery, anything) has produced a desired
  (vx, vy, wz) and the current `ranges` array contains at least one finite return
  below `range_max`. Precondition port: a desired twist is present on the
  blackboard AND `ranges` is fresh for this control step. It does NOT trigger on
  goal visibility, on `pose_error_estimate`, or on `contact` — it is unconditional
  with respect to all of those, which is the point: it is the last thing between
  any policy and the locomotion policy. If every beam is `inf` the filter is
  inert (dist saturates at range_max and no inequality binds), so it is still safe
  to leave permanently armed.

derivation: >
  MAPPING FROM THE PAPER TO THIS ROBOT. The paper's synchro-drive (v, w) maps onto
  (vx, wz) here. The paper's arcs assume "the translational velocity v always leads
  in the steering direction" (Section 3.1) — there is no lateral term in Eqs.
  (5)-(9), so the arc model simply cannot predict where a vy command sweeps. MY
  CHOICE, not the paper's: this leaf zeroes vy (emits vy = 0) rather than passing
  it through, because the dist() it computes would otherwise be a prediction about
  a path the robot is not taking. The paper's obstacle line field built from 24
  sonar beams with FIFO memory maps onto the 181 instantaneous lidar beams here;
  MY CHOICE: no FIFO memory is kept, only the current sweep, because the lidar
  gives a full circle every step and memory would inherit `pose_estimate` drift.
  This is why the mechanism is drift-immune: everything below is computed in the
  ROBOT frame from `ranges` and `range_angles`, and `pose_estimate` is never read.
  OBSTACLE POINTS. For each beam i with finite r_i <= range_max = 6.0 m, take
  p_i = (r_i*cos(a_i), r_i*sin(a_i)) in the robot frame. Inflate the body to a disc
  of radius rho = 0.38 m (MY NUMBER: Go2 body is about 0.70 m long by 0.31 m wide,
  circumscribed radius sqrt(0.35^2 + 0.155^2) ≈ 0.38 m). The paper's speed-dependent
  side clearance (Section 5.3) is deliberately NOT included here — it is a second
  mechanism and belongs on its own card.
  dist(vx, wz), following Section 5.2 / Figure 19:
    - straight case, |wz| < 1e-3 rad/s: over beams with |y_i| <= rho and x_i > 0,
      dist = min(x_i) - rho, clamped to [0, 6.0]; 6.0 if the set is empty.
    - arc case: r = vx / wz, centre C = (0, r) in the robot frame. Beam i lies in
      the swept annulus iff abs(norm(p_i - C) - |r|) <= rho. For those beams let
      gamma_i in [0, 2*pi) be the angle about C from the robot's current position
      to p_i, taken in the direction of travel (sign of wz, i.e. sign-corrected so
      an obstacle behind the sweep gives gamma near 2*pi, not near 0). Then, per the
      paper, the arc distance is gamma_i * |r|; take
      dist = min_i(gamma_i * |r|) - rho, clamped to [0, 6.0]; 6.0 if empty.
    - vx = 0 and |wz| >= 1e-3: pure spin sweeps no new ground for the disc model, so
      dist = 6.0 and only the wz inequality can bind (it will not, since it needs
      |wz| <= sqrt(2*6.0*wb_dot)). MY CHOICE.
  BRAKING ACCELERATIONS. The paper uses vb_dot = 50 cm/sec^2 and wb_dot = 60 deg/sec^2
  for RHINO (Example 1). Those are RHINO's, not a Go2's, and the true deceleration of
  the frozen locomotion policy is not observable through this interface. MY NUMBERS,
  chosen so the full command range is nulled in about one second of tracking:
  vb_dot = 0.8 m/s^2 (0.8 m/s -> 0 in 1.0 s) and wb_dot = 1.5 rad/s^2 (1.0 rad/s -> 0
  in 0.67 s). Consequence to check against behaviour: at full speed vx = 0.8 m/s the
  filter demands dist >= 0.8^2 / (2*0.8) = 0.40 m of arc clearance beyond the 0.38 m
  inflation, i.e. roughly 0.78 m of raw beam range ahead on the traced arc; at
  dist = 0.10 m the ceiling is sqrt(2*0.10*0.8) = 0.40 m/s. vb_dot is the single
  safety knob: halving it multiplies every permitted speed at a given distance by
  1/sqrt(2).
  APPLICATION. Given the desired (vx_d, vy_d, wz_d), first saturate to the interface
  limits (|vx| <= 0.8, |wz| <= 1.0), set vy = 0, then evaluate dist(vx, wz) on a
  grid of candidates vx in {0.0, 0.1, ..., 0.8} x wz in {-1.0, -0.9, ..., 1.0} and
  keep only pairs satisfying BOTH inequalities of Eq. (14) with |wz| in place of the
  paper's w. Emit the admissible pair minimising
  (vx - vx_d)^2 + (0.5*(wz - wz_d))^2 — MY CHOICE of tie-break, a nearest-point
  projection onto the admissible set, weighted so a rad/s of turn error costs half
  what a m/s of speed error costs; the intent is that the leaf changes the upstream
  command as little as admissibility allows, so the measured effect is attributable
  to Eq. (14) and not to a second objective smuggled in. (0.0, wz_d) is always in
  the candidate set, so a command always exists. The paper's dynamic window itself,
  Eq. (15) — restricting to velocities reachable within one interval given finite
  accelerations — is NOT part of this card; it is a separate mechanism.

prediction:
  statement: >
    With the braking-admissibility filter armed on top of an unchanged exploration
    driver, mean collisions per episode over the seed set drops by at least 50%
    relative to the reactive_avoid baseline on undisclosed-goal exploration
    scenarios, and this holds on the drifting-pose scenarios too, because the filter
    reads only robot-frame lidar. Falsified if the relative reduction is under 50%,
    or if collisions do not fall at all.
  metric: collisions
  baseline: reactive_avoid
  min_effect: 0.5
  cost_metric: time_to_goal

confidence: medium
```

What I did not know, stated plainly:

- **The braking accelerations are mine.** The paper gives RHINO's (50 cm/sec², 60 deg/sec², Example 1). A Go2 driven through a frozen locomotion policy exposes no deceleration limit at all — the Twist interface has no acceleration field and the policy's tracking transient is not in the observation. `vb_dot = 0.8 m/s²` and `wb_dot = 1.5 rad/s²` are assumptions about how fast that policy can null a command, and if it is slower than one second the filter is optimistic and the whole prediction fails in the unsafe direction. That is the number to attack first.
- **The footprint radius is mine**, from published Go2 body dimensions, not from anything in the document.
- **The lateral-velocity decision is mine and is a real loss.** DWA's arc model has no `vy`; I zero it rather than pass it through, which costs the quadruped a capability it actually has (strafing round obstacles). A holonomic extension of `dist()` would be a different card.
- **I dropped two things the paper has**: the speed-dependent side clearance and rotate-away mode (Section 5.3), and the dynamic window proper (Eq. 15). Each is a separate mechanism; bundling them would have made the unit scenario unable to isolate the claimed effect.
- **The goal-directed half of DWA does not survive the port at all.** The paper's objective function is dominated by `heading` (α = 0.8 vs β = γ = 0.1, Section 5.4), and `heading` needs a target point. In this task family `obs.goal` is `None` until latched, so that term has no argument — which is exactly why the card is built on the admissibility constraint, the part of DWA that is goal-free.
- The document does not state its publication venue, so the citation does not claim one.
